p5s0.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison album)
p5s0.text: Dark Horse is the fifth studio album by English musician George Harrison, released on Apple Records in December 1974 as the follow-up to "Living in the Material World".

p5s1.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison album)
p5s1.text: Although keenly anticipated on release, "Dark Horse" is associated with the controversial North American tour that Harrison staged with co-headliner Ravi Shankar in November and December that year.

p5s2.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison album)
p5s2.text: This was the first US tour by a member of the Beatles since 1966, and the public's nostalgia for the band, together with Harrison contracting laryngitis during rehearsals and choosing to feature Shankar so heavily in the program, resulted in scathing concert reviews from some influential music critics.

p8s0.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison song)
p8s0.text: "Dark Horse" is a song by English musician George Harrison, released as the title track to his 1974 solo album on Apple Records.

p8s1.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison song)
p8s1.text: The song was the album's lead single in North America, becoming a top-twenty hit in the United States, but it was Harrison's first single not to chart in Britain when issued there in February 1975.

p8s2.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison song)
p8s2.text: While the term "dark horse" had long been applied to Harrison due to his success as a solo artist following the Beatles' break-up in 1970, commentators recognise the song as Harrison's rebuttal to a number of possible detractors: those reviewers who criticised the spiritual content of his 1973 album "Living in the Material World"; his first wife, Pattie Boyd; and his former bandmates John Lennon and Paul McCartney.

p8s3.title: Dark Horse (George Harrison song)
p8s3.text: Harrison also used the title for that of his record label, and his 1974 North American tour with Ravi Shankar would come to be known as the Dark Horse Tour.

p1s0.title: Dark Horse Records

p1s1.title: Dark Horse Records
p1s1.text: The label's formation coincided with the winding down of the Beatles' Apple Records and allowed Harrison to continue supporting other artists' projects while maintaining his solo career.

p1s2.title: Dark Horse Records
p1s2.text: The initial signings were Indian musician Ravi Shankar and Splinter, the last of whom provided the label with its only significant commercial success until Harrison signed with Dark Horse in 1976.

p1s3.title: Dark Horse Records
p1s3.text: The label was distributed internationally by A&M Records for the first two years of its operation.

p1s4.title: Dark Horse Records
p1s4.text: Following a highly publicised split with A&M, Harrison and Dark Horse formed a long-term partnership with Warner Bros.

p1s5.title: Dark Horse Records
p1s5.text: Records that lasted until the expiration of his contract in 1994.

p6s2.title: The Dark Horse Years 1976–1992

p4s0.title: Grass Fight
p4s0.text: The Grass Fight was a small battle during the Texas Revolution, fought between the Mexican Army and the Texian Army.

p4s1.title: Grass Fight
p4s1.text: The battle took place on November 26, 1835, just south of San Antonio de Béxar in the Mexican region of Texas.

p4s2.title: Grass Fight
p4s2.text: The Texas Revolution had officially begun on October 2 and by the end of the month the Texian had initiated a siege of Béxar, home of the largest Mexican garrison in the province.

p4s3.title: Grass Fight
p4s3.text: Bored with the inactivity, many of the Texian soldiers returned home; a smaller number of adventurers from the United States arrived to replace them.

p4s4.title: Grass Fight
p4s4.text: After the Texian Army rejected commander-in-chief Stephen F. Austin's call to launch an assault on Béxar on November 22, Austin resigned from the army.

p4s5.title: Grass Fight
p4s5.text: The men elected Edward Burleson their new commander-in-chief.

p3s0.title: Battle of San Jacinto
p3s0.text: The Battle of San Jacinto, fought on April 21, 1836, in present-day Harris County, Texas, was the decisive battle of the Texas Revolution.

p3s1.title: Battle of San Jacinto
p3s1.text: Led by General Sam Houston, the Texian Army engaged and defeated General Antonio López de Santa Anna's Mexican army in a fight that lasted just 18 minutes.

p5s0.title: Runaway Scrape
p5s0.text: The Runaway Scrape events took place mainly between September 1835 and April 1836, and were the evacuations by Texas residents fleeing the Mexican Army of Operations during the Texas Revolution, from the Battle of the Alamo through the decisive Battle of San Jacinto.

p5s1.title: Runaway Scrape
p5s1.text: The "ad interim" government of the new Republic of Texas and much of the civilian population fled eastward ahead of the Mexican forces.

p5s2.title: Runaway Scrape
p5s2.text: The conflict arose after Antonio López de Santa Anna abrogated the 1824 constitution of Mexico and established martial law in Coahuila y Tejas.

p5s3.title: Runaway Scrape
p5s3.text: The Texians resisted and declared their independence.

p5s4.title: Runaway Scrape
p5s4.text: It was Sam Houston's responsibility, as the appointed commander-in-chief of the Provisional Army of Texas (before such an army actually existed), to recruit and train a military force to defend the population against troops led by Santa Anna.

p0s0.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s0.text: The Siege of Béxar (or Bejar) was an early campaign of the Texas Revolution in which a volunteer Texian army defeated Mexican forces at San Antonio de Béxar (now San Antonio, Texas, US).

p0s1.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s1.text: Texians had become disillusioned with the Mexican government as President and General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna's tenure became increasingly dictatorial.

p0s2.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s2.text: In early October, 1835, Texas settlers gathered in Gonzales to stop Mexican troops from reclaiming a small cannon.

p0s3.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s3.text: The resulting skirmish, known as the Battle of Gonzales, launched the Texas Revolution.

p0s4.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s4.text: Men continued to assemble in Gonzales and soon established the Texian Army.

p0s5.title: Siege of Béxar
p0s5.text: Despite a lack of military training, well-respected local leader General Stephen F. Austin was elected commander.

p2s0.title: José de Urrea
p2s0.text: José de Urrea (March 19, 1797 – August 1, 1849) was a Mexican general.

p2s1.title: José de Urrea
p2s1.text: He fought under General Antonio López de Santa Anna during the Texas Revolution.

p2s2.title: José de Urrea
p2s2.text: Urrea's forces were never defeated in battle during the Texas Revolution.

p2s3.title: José de Urrea
p2s3.text: His most notable success was that of the Goliad Campaign, in which James Fannin's 400 soldiers were surrounded and induced to capitulate under terms, but were massacred in Urrea's absence on the orders of Santa Anna.

p2s4.title: José de Urrea
p2s4.text: Urrea also fought in the Mexican-American War.

p1s0.title: Fort Bend
p1s0.text: Fort Bend was a blockhouse built in a large bend of the Brazos River in what is now Fort Bend County, Texas, to provide protection against Indian raids.

p1s1.title: Fort Bend
p1s1.text: It was erected in November 1822 by several members of Stephen F. Austin's Old Three Hundred, including William W. Little, Joseph Polley, William Smithers[Smeathers], Charles Beard, Henry Holster and is described as a "little log shanty."

p1s2.title: Fort Bend
p1s2.text: The location was reportedly selected by Austin, and a settlement soon grew up around the post.

p1s3.title: Fort Bend
p1s3.text: As the site provided one of the more favorable fords of the Brazos River, it became important during the Texas Revolution.

p1s4.title: Fort Bend
p1s4.text: The Fort Bend crossing was briefly defended in April 1836 by a rear guard detachment led by Wiley Martin.

p1s5.title: Fort Bend
p1s5.text: After Martin was maneuvered out of the position Gen. Antonio López de Santa Anna transported a portion of his Mexican army across the Brazos at the crossing.

p1s6.title: Fort Bend
p1s6.text: After Santa Anna's defeat at the battle of San Jacinto the site was used briefly by the Texas army.

p1s7.title: Fort Bend
p1s7.text: Troops under Thomas Jefferson Green, who were in pursuit of retreating Mexican forces led by Gen. Vicente Filisola, halted for a short time in mid-May 1836 at Fort Bend.

p1s8.title: Fort Bend
p1s8.text: Because Fort Bend had been the center of activity in the area its name was given to the county when it was established in 1837.

p1s9.title: Fort Bend
p1s9.text: The next year nearby Richmond, Texas was selected as the county seat and soon absorbed the smaller Fort Bend settlement.

p1s10.title: Fort Bend
p1s10.text: In 1936 the Texas Centennial Commission erected a monument to commemorate Fort Bend's role in the Texas Revolution.

p7s0.title: Army of the Republic of Texas
p7s0.text: The Army of the Republic of Texas was the land-based component of the armed forces for the Republic of Texas.

p7s1.title: Army of the Republic of Texas
p7s1.text: It directly descended from the Texian Army, which was established on October 2, 1835, to fight for independence from Mexico in the Texas Revolution.

p7s2.title: Army of the Republic of Texas
p7s2.text: The army was provisionally formed from the Consultation in November 1835, and officially established on September 5, 1836, from Article II, Section 5 of the Constitution of the Republic of Texas.

p7s3.title: Army of the Republic of Texas
p7s3.text: After Texas' annexation by the United States, the Army of the Republic of Texas was merged into the United States Army.

p7s4.title: Army of the Republic of Texas
p7s4.text: Today, the 141st Infantry Regiment trace their lineage back to the Texas Revolution.

p6s1.text: The settlement was established in 1834 by Sterling C. Robertson and named for his mother Mrs. Sarah (née Maclin) Robertson and Agustín Viesca, the Mexican governor of Coahuila y Tejas.

p0s0.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s0.text: Rear Admiral George Heneage Lawrence Dundas CB (8 September 1778 – 7 October 1834) was a senior officer in the Royal Navy.

p0s1.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s1.text: As a junior officer he came to prominence due to his brave conduct during a fire on the first-rate HMS "Queen Charlotte".

p0s2.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s2.text: As a result of this he was appointed to the command of the sixth-rate HMS "Calpe" in which he took part in the Battle of Algeciras Bay in July 1801 during the French Revolutionary Wars.

p0s3.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s3.text: After serving for four years as Whig Member of Parliament for Richmond, he was given command of the fifth-rate HMS "Euryalus" and took part in the unsuccessful Walcheren Campaign in July 1809 during the Napoleonic Wars.

p0s4.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s4.text: He transferred to the third-rate HMS "Edinburgh" and landed troops at Viareggio in Italy in November 1812 later in that War.

p0s5.title: George Heneage Lawrence Dundas
p0s5.text: He went on to be Member of Parliament for Orkney and Shetland and became First Naval Lord in the First Melbourne ministry in August 1834 but died in office just two months later in October 1834.

p8s0.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s0.text: Convoy TM 1 was the code name for an Allied convoy during the Second World War.

p8s1.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s1.text: Nine tankers, escorted by Royal Navy warships, attempted to reach Gibraltar from Trinidad.

p8s2.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s2.text: The convoy was attacked by a U-boat wolf pack in the central Atlantic Ocean, and most of the merchant vessels were sunk.

p8s3.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s3.text: This was one of the most successful attacks on Allied supply convoys throughout the entire war.

p8s4.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s4.text: The convoy was defended by the destroyer HMS "Havelock", and three Flower class corvettes, HMS "Godetia" , HMS "Pimpernel" and HMS "Saxifrage".

p8s5.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s5.text: Seven tankers were sunk during the attacks, two surviving to reach Gibraltar.

p8s6.title: Convoy TM 1
p8s6.text: Two U-boats were damaged during the attacks.

p7s0.title: World War I
p7s0.text: World War I (WWI or WW1), also known as the First World War, the Great War, or the War to End All Wars, was a global war originating in Europe that lasted from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918.

p7s1.title: World War I
p7s1.text: More than 70 million military personnel, including 60 million Europeans, were mobilised in one of the largest wars in history.

p7s2.title: World War I
p7s2.text: Over nine million combatants and seven million civilians died as a result of the war (including the victims of a number of genocides), a casualty rate exacerbated by the belligerents' technological and industrial sophistication, and the tactical stalemate caused by gruelling trench warfare.

p7s3.title: World War I
p7s3.text: It was one of the deadliest conflicts in history, and paved the way for major political changes, including revolutions in many of the nations involved.

p7s4.title: World War I
p7s4.text: Unresolved rivalries still extant at the end of the conflict contributed to the start of the Second World War only twenty-one years later.

p9s0.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s0.text: William Brown (8 May 1764 – 20 September 1814) was an officer of the British Royal Navy who served in increasingly senior positions during a long period from the American Revolutionary War, including the French Revolutionary War, and until the Napoleonic Wars.

p9s1.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s1.text: He began his naval career as a servant to Captain Philemon Pownoll in the frigate HMS Apollo and became a midshipman after two years.

p9s2.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s2.text: He then served on HMS Resolution with Lord Robert Manners and came home with him in HMS Andromache.

p9s3.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s3.text: He spent the next five years ashore in peacetime.

p9s4.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s4.text: After a brief time on HMS Bounty he was taken off by the First lord and moved to HMS Ariel before the Bounty sailed.

p9s5.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s5.text: He was then moved to HMS Leander, where he was commissioned by Admiral Peyton in 1788.

p9s6.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s6.text: He later captained a series of ships serving in the Mediterranean, the North Sea, the Channel Fleet and then the Mediterranean, again with lord St Vincent.

p9s7.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s7.text: He captained HMS Ajax in the Blockade of Brest and the Battle of Cape Finisterre and then at Cadiz at Nelson's personal request.

p9s8.title: William Brown (Royal Navy officer)
p9s8.text: After Trafalgar he had a series of shore postings as Dockyard Commissioner at Malta and Shearness before being made Commander in Chief of the Channel Islands and then Jamaica where he died.

p6s0.title: Escapees' Medal
p6s0.text: The Escapees' Medal (French: "Médaille des Évadés" ) is a military award bestowed by the government of France to individuals who were prisoners of war and who successfully escaped internment or died as a result of their escape attempt.

p6s1.title: Escapees' Medal
p6s1.text: The "Escapees' Medal" was established by a 1926 law, intended to honour combatants not only of the First World War, but also of the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.

p6s2.title: Escapees' Medal
p6s2.text: Its statute was later amended to include combatants of the Second World War and later conflicts.

p2s0.title: Timeline of the Holocaust
p2s0.text: A timeline of the Holocaust is detailed in the events listed below.

p2s1.title: Timeline of the Holocaust
p2s1.text: Also referred to as the Shoah (in Hebrew), the Holocaust was a genocide in which some six million European Jews were killed by Nazi Germany and its World War II collaborators.

p2s2.title: Timeline of the Holocaust
p2s2.text: About 1.5 million of the victims were children.

p2s3.title: Timeline of the Holocaust
p2s3.text: Two-thirds of the nine million Jews who had resided in Europe were murdered.

p2s4.title: Timeline of the Holocaust
p2s4.text: The following timeline has been compiled from a variety of sources including the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum.

p5s0.title: The Holocaust
p5s0.text: The Holocaust, also referred to as the Shoah, was a genocide in which Adolf Hitler's Nazi Germany and its World War II collaborators killed some six million European Jews.

p5s1.title: The Holocaust
p5s1.text: The victims included 1.5 million children and constituted about two-thirds of the nine million Jews in Continental Europe.

p5s2.title: The Holocaust
p5s2.text: A broader definition of the Holocaust includes non-Jewish victims such as the Roma, ethnic Poles, other Slavic ethnic groups, and the disabled and mentally ill.

p5s3.title: The Holocaust
p5s3.text: An even broader definition includes Soviet citizens and prisoners of war, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses, black people, and political opponents of the Nazis.

p9s0.title: Frederick Walton (engineer)
p9s0.text: Frederick Thomas Granville Walton CIE, M. Inst C.E., Telford Medal, was a notable British railway engineer in India.

p9s1.title: Frederick Walton (engineer)
p9s1.text: He specialised in bridge construction.

p9s2.title: Frederick Walton (engineer)
p9s2.text: He was commonly known by his middle name Granville, and was often referred to as Mr F.T.G. Walton.

p9s3.title: Frederick Walton (engineer)
p9s3.text: Walton was born in September 1840 in Hampton, Middlesex, England to William Walton (1795–1889) of Reading, Berkshire and Elizabeth Louisa Plunkett (1801–1866) originally of Dalston, Cumberland.

p0s0.title: Maurice Ravel
p0s0.text: Joseph Maurice Ravel (] ; 7 March 1875 – 28 December 1937) was a French composer, pianist and conductor.

p0s1.title: Maurice Ravel
p0s1.text: He is often associated with impressionism along with his elder contemporary Claude Debussy, although both composers rejected the term.

p0s2.title: Maurice Ravel
p0s2.text: In the 1920s and 1930s Ravel was internationally regarded as France's greatest living composer.

p7s0.title: Piano Trio (Ravel)
p7s0.text: Maurice Ravel's Piano Trio for piano, violin and cello is a chamber work composed in 1914.

p7s1.title: Piano Trio (Ravel)
p7s1.text: Dedicated to Ravel's counterpoint teacher André Gedalge, the trio was first performed in Paris in January 1915, by Alfredo Casella (piano), Gabriel Willaume (violin), and Louis Feuillard (cello).

p7s2.title: Piano Trio (Ravel)
p7s2.text: A typical performance of the work lasts about 30 minutes.

p6s0.title: William Walton
p6s0.text: Sir William Turner Walton, OM (29 March 19028 March 1983) was an English composer.

p6s1.title: William Walton
p6s1.text: During a sixty-year career, he wrote music in several classical genres and styles, from film scores to opera.

p6s2.title: William Walton
p6s2.text: His best-known works include "Façade", the cantata "Belshazzar's Feast", the Viola Concerto and the First Symphony.

p1s0.title: Histoires naturelles
p1s0.text: Histoires naturelles ("Natural Histories") is a song cycle by Maurice Ravel, composed in 1906.

p1s1.title: Histoires naturelles
p1s1.text: It sets five poems by Jules Renard to music for voice and piano.

p1s2.title: Histoires naturelles
p1s2.text: Ravel's pupil Manuel Rosenthal created a version for voice and orchestra.

p1s3.title: Histoires naturelles
p1s3.text: The cycle is dedicated to the mezzo-soprano Jane Bathori, who gave the first performance, accompanied by the composer, on 12 January 1907.

p8s0.title: L'enfant et les sortilèges
p8s0.text: L'enfant et les sortilèges: Fantaisie lyrique en deux parties ("The Child and the Spells: A Lyric Fantasy in Two Parts") is an opera in one act, with music by Maurice Ravel to a libretto by Colette.

p8s1.title: L'enfant et les sortilèges
p8s1.text: It is Ravel's second opera, his first being "L'heure espagnole".

p8s2.title: L'enfant et les sortilèges
p8s2.text: Written from 1917 to 1925, "L'enfant et les sortilèges" was first performed in Monte Carlo in 1925 under the baton of Victor de Sabata.

p4s0.title: Shéhérazade (Ravel)
p4s0.text: Shéhérazade is the title of two works by the French composer Maurice Ravel.

p4s1.title: Shéhérazade (Ravel)
p4s1.text: Both have their origins in the composer's fascination with Scheherazade, the heroine and narrator of "The Arabian Nights".

p4s2.title: Shéhérazade (Ravel)
p4s2.text: The first work, an overture (1898), Ravel's earliest surviving orchestral piece, was not well received at its premiere and has not subsequently been among his most popular works.

p4s3.title: Shéhérazade (Ravel)
p4s3.text: Four years later he had a much greater success with a song cycle with the same title, which has remained a standard repertoire piece and has been recorded many times.

p5s0.title: Rapsodie espagnole
p5s0.text: Rapsodie espagnole is an orchestral rhapsody written by Maurice Ravel.

p5s1.title: Rapsodie espagnole
p5s1.text: Composed between 1907 and 1908, the "Rapsodie" is one of Ravel's first major works for orchestra.

p5s2.title: Rapsodie espagnole
p5s2.text: It was first performed in Paris in 1908 and quickly entered the international repertoire.

p5s3.title: Rapsodie espagnole
p5s3.text: The piece draws on the composer's Spanish heritage, and is one of several of his works set in or reflecting Spain.

p3s0.title: Jeux d'eau (Ravel)
p3s0.text: Jeux d’eau (] ) is a piece for solo piano by Maurice Ravel.

p3s1.title: Jeux d'eau (Ravel)
p3s1.text: The title is often translated as "Fountains", "Playing water" or literally "Water Games" (see "Jeux d'eau", water features in gardens).

p3s2.title: Jeux d'eau (Ravel)
p3s2.text: At the time of writing "Jeux d'eau", Ravel was a student of Gabriel Fauré, to whom the piece is dedicated.

p3s3.title: Jeux d'eau (Ravel)
p3s3.text: Pianist Ricardo Viñes was the first to publicly perform the work in 1902, although it had been privately performed for Les Apaches previously.

p9s0.title: I Drink My Coffee Alone
p9s0.text: I Drink My Coffee Alone is a one-man deathcore/electronic project from Trier, Germany, formed by Alex Gazin in 2011, significantly noted for his dominating growls and use of electronic instrumentation.

p9s1.title: I Drink My Coffee Alone
p9s1.text: Gazin has previously released one EP and two full-length albums.

p1s0.title: Šešupė
p1s0.text: The Šešupė ( ; Russian: Шешупе ; German: "Scheschup(p)e" ; Polish: "Szeszupa" ) is a river that flows through Poland (27 km), Lithuania (158 km), and Russia (62 km).

p1s1.title: Šešupė
p1s1.text: The river flows for 51 km along the border between the Kaliningrad Oblast, an exclave of Russia, and Lithuania.

p1s2.title: Šešupė
p1s2.text: The Šešupė originates near the Polish town of Szeszupka, about 10 miles from the Polish-Lithuanian border, and flows into the Nemunas near the town of Neman on the border between Lithuania and Kaliningrad Oblast.

p8s0.title: Ledava
p8s0.text: The Ledava is the largest river of Goričko, northeastern Slovenia, and the largest tributary of the Mur River in Slovenia.

p8s1.title: Ledava
p8s1.text: The river is 76 km in length.

p8s2.title: Ledava
p8s2.text: It originates in Austria as the "Lendva Bach" and first flows southeast.

p8s3.title: Ledava
p8s3.text: It enters Slovenia near Kugla Hill, the highest peak of Prekmurje (418 m ), and flows south as the "Ledava".

p8s4.title: Ledava
p8s4.text: In this part of its course it forms the only gorge in Goričko.

p8s5.title: Ledava
p8s5.text: In the village of Ropoča it flows into the Ledava Reservoir, which distinguishes itself by a variety of bird species, a variety of dragonflies, and the best preserved otter population in Slovenia.

p8s6.title: Ledava
p8s6.text: The Ledava is the only outflow from the lake.

p8s7.title: Ledava
p8s7.text: In its lower course the river flows through Murska Sobota and Lendava.

p8s8.title: Ledava
p8s8.text: It has several (mainly left) tributaries in this part, the largest of them being the Big Krka and the longest Kobilje Creek.

p6s0.title: Cheakamus River
p6s0.text: The Cheakamus River (pron.

p6s1.title: Cheakamus River
p6s1.text: CHEEK-a-mus) is a tributary of the Squamish River, beginning on the west slopes of Outlier Peak in Garibaldi Provincial Park upstream from Cheakamus Lake on the southeastern outskirts of the resort area of Whistler.

p6s2.title: Cheakamus River
p6s2.text: The river flows into Cheakamus Lake before exiting it and flowing northwest until it turns south and enters Daisy Lake.

p6s3.title: Cheakamus River
p6s3.text: Between the outlet of Daisy Lake and its mouth, much of its length is spent going through Cheakamus Canyon, where the river flows through swift rapids and even one good sized waterfall.

p6s4.title: Cheakamus River
p6s4.text: The river flows south from the lake and through the canyon before joining the Squamish River at Cheekye, a few miles north of the town of Squamish.

p6s5.title: Cheakamus River
p6s5.text: The river's name is an anglicization of the name of Chiyakmesh ("people of the fish weir"), a village of the Squamish people and a reserve of the Squamish Nation.

p5s0.title: Trier
p5s0.text: Trier (] ; Luxembourgish: "Tréier" ] ), formerly known in English as Treves (French: "Trèves" , ] ) and Triers (see also names in other languages), is a city in Germany on the banks of the Moselle.

p5s1.title: Trier
p5s1.text: Trier lies in a valley between low vine-covered hills of red sandstone in the west of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the border with Luxembourg and within the important Moselle wine region.

p0s0.title: Sonthi River
p0s0.text: The Sonthi River (Thai: ลำสนธิ , rtgs: "Lam Sonthi" ,  ] ) is a tributary of the Pa Sak River.

p0s1.title: Sonthi River
p0s1.text: It originates at the Ruak and Phanghoei mountains in the border area of Lam Sonthi district, Lopburi province and Si Thep, Phetchabun province.

p0s2.title: Sonthi River
p0s2.text: The river flows southward as the backbone of Lam Sonthi district and joins with the Phaya Klang River from Muak Lek district, Saraburi province.

p0s3.title: Sonthi River
p0s3.text: Then the river flows ahead to west and tributes the Pa Sak River in Chai Badan.

p0s4.title: Sonthi River
p0s4.text: It is 70 km long.

p2s0.title: Ramganga
p2s0.text: Ramganga West River originates from Doodhatoli ranges in the district of Pauri Garhwal, Uttarakhand state of India.

p2s1.title: Ramganga
p2s1.text: The Ramganga River flows to south west from Kumaun Himalaya.

p2s2.title: Ramganga
p2s2.text: It is a tributary of the river Ganges, originates from the high altitude zone of 800m-900m.

p2s3.title: Ramganga
p2s3.text: Ramganga flows by the Corbett National Park near Ramnagar of Nainital district from where it descends upon the plains.

p2s4.title: Ramganga
p2s4.text: Moradabad, Bareilly, Badaun, Shahjahanpur and Hardoi cities of Uttar Pradesh is situated on its banks.

p2s5.title: Ramganga
p2s5.text: The Ramganga Dam crosses the river at Kalagarh for irrigation and hydroelectric generation.

p2s6.title: Ramganga
p2s6.text: An annual festival of Ganga Dassahra is organised on its banks annually during the months of September and October at Chaubari village near Bareilly.

p2s7.title: Ramganga
p2s7.text: It has a drainage basin of 30,641 km.

p3s0.title: Mthatha River
p3s0.text: Mthatha River or Umtata River (Xhosa: "<nowiki>'</nowiki>mtathe Bawo" ) is a river in the Eastern Cape Province in South Africa.

p3s1.title: Mthatha River
p3s1.text: The river flows into the Indian Ocean in an estuary located near Coffee Bay.

p3s2.title: Mthatha River
p3s2.text: The Mthatha river flows in a southeastern direction and is approximately 250 km long with a catchment area of 2,600 km².

p3s3.title: Mthatha River
p3s3.text: It is named after Mthatha Town (Umtata).

p7s0.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s0.text: Kosasthalaiyar River, also known as "'Kortalaiyar" in Manali a distributary, is one of the three rivers that flow in the Chennai metropolitan area.

p7s1.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s1.text: The 136 km river originates near pallipet in thiruvallur District and drains into the Bay of Bengal.

p7s2.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s2.text: Its northern tributary Nagari river originates in Chitoor district of Andhra Pradesh and joins the main river in the back waters of Poondy dam.

p7s3.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s3.text: Its catchment area spreads in Vellore, Chitoor, North Arcot, Thiruvallur and Chennai districts.

p7s4.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s4.text: It has catchment area in North Arcot District with a branch near Kesavaram Anicut and flows to the city as Cooum River and the main Kosasthalaiyar River flows to Poondi reservoir.

p7s5.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s5.text: From Poondi reservoir, the river flows through Thiruvallur District, enters the Chennai metropolitan area, and joins the sea at Ennore creek.

p7s6.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s6.text: There are two check dams across the river at Tamaraipakkam and Vallur.

p7s7.title: Kosasthalaiyar River
p7s7.text: The excess discharge in the river is controlled by the Tamarapakkam Anicut located across the river in the downstream of Poondi reservoir.

p4s0.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p4s2.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p4s4.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p4s6.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p4s9.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p4s10.title: Lakers–Clippers rivalry

p7s0.text: The Ganghwa massacre (Korean: 강화 양민학살 사건 , Hanja: 江華良民虐殺事件) was a massacre conducted by the South Korean forces, South Korean Police forces and pro-South Korean militiamen, between 6 and 9 January 1951, of 212 to 1,300 unarmed civilians in the Ganghwa county of the Incheon metropolitan city in South Korea.

p7s1.title: Ganghwa massacre

p8s0.text: The Ganghwa Island incident or the Japanese Battle of Ganghwa (Korean: 운요호 사건 [雲揚號事件] "Unyo-ho sageon" meaning ""Un'yō" incident"; Japanese: 事件 "Kōkatō jiken"), was a purposely armed clash between the Joseon Dynasty of Korea and Japan which occurred in the vicinity of Ganghwa Island on September 20, 1875.

p9s0.title: Bodo League massacre

p9s1.title: Bodo League massacre
p9s1.text: Estimates of the death toll vary.

p9s2.title: Bodo League massacre

p9s4.title: Bodo League massacre
p9s4.text: The massacre was wrongly blamed on the communists.

p9s5.title: Bodo League massacre
p9s5.text: For four decades the South Korean government concealed this massacre.

p9s6.title: Bodo League massacre

p9s7.title: Bodo League massacre

p3s0.title: 1991 Kokkadichcholai massacre

p2s7.text: In 1965, a modern publishing facility was built for Herald House on Noland Road in Independence.

p2s8.title: Herald House
p2s8.text: That facility was closed in 1999 and printing has been outsourced since that date.

p2s9.title: Herald House
p2s9.text: The publishing offices were moved to The Temple and The Auditorium in Independence, Missouri.

p1s0.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s0.text: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone is a park in Monroe, Connecticut, United States.

p1s1.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s1.text: Its mission is to provide excellence in outdoor education and to promote exploration and learning in a fun, hands-on environment as a prototype for the Federal No Child Left Inside initiative.

p1s2.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s2.text: The park covers 170 acre and has 3 loop trails, each with marked interpretive signs.

p1s3.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s3.text: There is also an outdoor classroom for schools and groups, and a scavenger hunt scorecard.

p1s4.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s4.text: The park provides additional educational resources for teachers, as well as programs for school groups, daycare centers, and scouts.

p1s5.title: Webb Mountain Discovery Zone
p1s5.text: The park is owned by the Town of Monroe and administered by the Friends of Webb Mountain.

p8s0.title: Aliso Canyon Oil Field
p8s0.text: The Aliso Canyon Oil Field (also Aliso Canyon Natural Gas Storage Field, Aliso Canyon Underground Storage Facility) is an oil field and natural gas storage facility in the Santa Susana Mountains in Los Angeles County, California, north of the Porter Ranch neighborhood of the City of Los Angeles.

p8s1.title: Aliso Canyon Oil Field
p8s1.text: Discovered in 1938 and quickly developed afterward, the field peaked as an oil producer in the 1950s, but has remained active since its discovery.

p8s2.title: Aliso Canyon Oil Field
p8s2.text: One of its depleted oil and gas producing formations, the Sesnon-Frew zone, was converted into a gas storage reservoir in 1973 by the Southern California Gas Company, the gas utility servicing the southern half of California.

p8s3.title: Aliso Canyon Oil Field
p8s3.text: This reservoir is the second-largest natural gas storage site in the western United States, with a capacity of over 86 billion cubic feet of natural gas.

p8s4.title: Aliso Canyon Oil Field
p8s4.text: Currently it is one of four gas storage facilities owned by Southern California Gas, the others being the La Goleta Gas Field west of Santa Barbara, Honor Rancho near Newhall, and Playa del Rey.

p3s0.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone
p3s0.text: The Great Falls Tectonic Zone is a major intracontinental shear zone between the Hearne craton and Wyoming craton basement rock of the Archean Eon which form part of the North American continent.

p3s1.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone
p3s1.text: The zone is an area about 100 miles (150 km) wide extending from the southwestern Idaho-Montana border across Montana to the northwestern Montana-Saskatchewan-North Dakota border.

p3s2.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone
p3s2.text: It is named for the Great Falls of the Missouri River, a major geologic feature of the area.

p3s3.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone
p3s3.text: The central and western portions of the zone are believed to be about 1.1 to 3.3 billion years old.

p3s4.title: Great Falls Tectonic Zone
p3s4.text: The central part of the zone lacks Archean rock, however, leading at least one group of scientists to speculate that it was formed very late in the Paleoproterozoic Era.

p5s0.title: Centaurium
p5s0.text: Centaurium (Centaury) is a genus of 20 species in the gentian family (Gentianaceae), tribe Chironieae, subtribe Chironiinae.

p5s1.title: Centaurium
p5s1.text: The genus was named after the centaur Chiron, famed in Greek mythology for his skill in medicinal herbs.

p5s2.title: Centaurium
p5s2.text: It is distributed across Europe and into Asia.

p2s0.title: Dacrydium
p2s0.text: Dacrydium is a genus of conifers belonging to the podocarp family Podocarpaceae.

p2s1.title: Dacrydium
p2s1.text: Sixteen species of evergreen dioecious trees and shrubs are presently recognized.

p2s2.title: Dacrydium
p2s2.text: The genus was first described by Solander in 1786, and formerly included many more species, which were divided into sections A, B, and C by Florin in 1931.

p2s3.title: Dacrydium
p2s3.text: The revisions of de Laubenfels and Quinn (see references), reclassified the former section A as the new genus "Falcatifolium", divided Section C into new genera "Lepidothamnus, Lagarostrobos" and "Halocarpus", and retained Section B as genus "Dacrydium".

p7s0.title: Centaurium pulchellum
p7s0.text: Centaurium pulchellum is a species of flowering plant in the gentian family known by the common name lesser centaury.

p7s1.title: Centaurium pulchellum
p7s1.text: It differs from "Centaurium erythraea" by lacking basal rosette of leaves and by having a developed peduncle below the flowers.

p7s2.title: Centaurium pulchellum
p7s2.text: It is often much smaller, less than ten centimetres.

p3s0.title: Flora of Western Australia
p3s0.text: The flora of Western Australia comprises 10,252 published native vascular plant species and a further 1,245 unpublished species.

p3s1.title: Flora of Western Australia
p3s1.text: They occur within 1,543 genera from 211 families; there are also 1,276 naturalised alien or invasive plant species more commonly known as weeds.

p3s2.title: Flora of Western Australia
p3s2.text: There are an estimated 150,000 cryptogam species or nonvascular plants which include lichens, and fungi although only 1,786 species have been published, with 948 algae and 672 lichen the majority.

p9s0.title: Plant cover
p9s0.text: The abundances of plant species are often measured by plant cover, i.e. the relative area covered by different plant species in a small plot.

p9s1.title: Plant cover
p9s1.text: Plant cover is not biased by the size and distributions of individuals, and is an important and often measured characteristic of the composition of plant communities.

p9s2.title: Plant cover
p9s2.text: Plant cover data may be used to classify the studied plant community into a vegetation type, to test different ecological hypothesis on plant abundance, and in gradient studies, where the effects of different environmental gradients on the abundance of specific plant species are investigated.

p6s0.title: Flora of India
p6s0.text: The flora of India is one of the richest in the world due to the wide range of climate, topology and habitat in the country.

p6s1.title: Flora of India
p6s1.text: There are estimated to be over 16,000 species of flowering plants in India, which constitute some 6-7 percent of the total plant species in the world.

p6s2.title: Flora of India
p6s2.text: India is home to more than 45,000 species of plants, including a variety of endemics.

p6s3.title: Flora of India
p6s3.text: The use of plants as a source of medicines has been an integral part of life in India from the earliest times.

p6s4.title: Flora of India
p6s4.text: There are more than 3000 Indian plant species officially documented as possessing great medicinal potential.

p6s5.title: Flora of India
p6s5.text: India is divided into eight main floristic regions : Western Himalayas, Eastern Himalayas, Assam, Indus plain, Ganges plain, the Deccan, Malabar and the Andaman Islands.

p4s0.title: Flora of Lebanon
p4s0.text: The flora of Lebanon" includes approximately 2,600 plant species.

p4s1.title: Flora of Lebanon
p4s1.text: Situated on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Basin", Lebanon is a reservoir of plant diversity and one of the world's Biodiversity hotspots for conservation priorities.

p4s2.title: Flora of Lebanon
p4s2.text: Endemic species constitute 12% of the Lebanese flora, 221 plant species are broad endemics and 90 are narrow endemics.

p8s0.title: Wildlife of Burkina Faso
p8s0.text: Burkina Faso is largely wild bush country with a mixture of grass and small trees in varying proportions.

p8s1.title: Wildlife of Burkina Faso
p8s1.text: The savanna region is mainly grassland in the rainy season and semi desert during the harmattan period (defined as the period when stormy and dusty Sahara winds blow dry and hot).

p8s2.title: Wildlife of Burkina Faso
p8s2.text: Fauna, one of the most diverse in West Africa, includes the elephant, hippopotamus, buffalo, monkey, lions, crocodile, giraffe, various types of antelope, and a vast variety of bird and insect life.

p8s3.title: Wildlife of Burkina Faso
p8s3.text: The country has 147 mammal species, 330 aquatic species including 121 species of fish and 2067 different plant species.

p8s4.title: Wildlife of Burkina Faso
p8s4.text: Of the plant species, the dominant endemic species are shea tree "(Butyrospermum parkii") and the baobab, the former plant species has immense economic value to the country.

p0s0.title: Halophyte
p0s0.text: A halophyte is a plant that grows in waters of high salinity, coming into contact with saline water through its roots or by salt spray, such as in saline semi-deserts, mangrove swamps, marshes and sloughs and seashores.

p0s1.title: Halophyte
p0s1.text: The word derives from Ancient Greek ἅλας (halas) 'salt' and φυτόν (phyton) 'plant'.

p0s2.title: Halophyte
p0s2.text: An example of a halophyte is the salt marsh grass "Spartina alterniflora" (smooth cordgrass).

p0s3.title: Halophyte
p0s3.text: Relatively few plant species are halophytes—perhaps only 2% of all plant species.

p1s0.title: The Cult
p1s0.text: The Cult are a British rock band formed in 1983.

p1s1.title: The Cult
p1s1.text: Before settling on their current name in January 1984, the band performed under the name Death Cult, which was an evolution of the name of lead singer Ian Astbury's previous band Southern Death Cult.

p1s2.title: The Cult
p1s2.text: They gained a dedicated following in the UK in the mid-1980s as a post-punk/gothic rock band, with singles such as "She Sells Sanctuary", before breaking mainstream in the United States in the late 1980s as a hard rock band with singles such as "Love Removal Machine" and "Fire Woman".

p1s3.title: The Cult
p1s3.text: According to music critic Stephen Thomas Erlewine, the band fuse a "heavy metal revivalist" sound with the "pseudo-mysticism ... of The Doors [and] the guitar-orchestrations of Led Zeppelin ... while adding touches of post-punk goth rock".

p1s4.title: The Cult
p1s4.text: Since the initial formation of Southern Death Cult in Bradford in 1981, the band have had various line-ups; the longest-serving members are Astbury and guitarist Billy Duffy, the band's two songwriters.

p5s0.title: Progres 2
p5s0.text: Progres 2 is an art rock band from Brno, Czech Republic.

p5s1.title: Progres 2
p5s1.text: It was established in 1968, known as Progress Organization, by Zdeněk Kluka, Pavel Váně, Jan Sochor and Emanuel Sideridis.

p5s2.title: Progres 2
p5s2.text: Its most important album in a Czech context was the rock opera project "Dialog s vesmírem" (Dialog with The Universe) in 1978, only a year after the transformation of the band called "Bardonaj" to the new band Progres 2.

p5s3.title: Progres 2
p5s3.text: The public presentation of this rock opera was the first audiovisual program of rock music in Czechoslovakia, inspired by the British rock group Pink Floyd.

p5s4.title: Progres 2

p5s5.title: Progres 2

p5s8.title: Progres 2

p3s2.text: Formed from a school band called Painted Lady, Girlschool enjoyed strong media exposure and commercial success in the UK in the early 1980s with three albums of 'punk-tinged metal' and a few singles, but lost their momentum in the following years.

p9s0.title: Aaron Buchanan & The Cult Classics
p9s0.text: Aaron Buchanan & The Cult Classics are a British rock band formed in 2016 by former Heaven's Basement vocalist of international acclaim (and Red Bull Records alumnus), Aaron Buchanan.

p9s1.text: Band members include Aaron Buchanan (vocals), Laurie Buchanan (guitar and vocals), Tom McCarthy (guitar), Chris Guyatt (bass) and Paul White (drums) (formally of industrial metal band The Defiled).

p1s0.title: Victoria Hanley
p1s0.text: Victoria Hanley is an American young adult fantasy novelist.

p1s1.title: Victoria Hanley
p1s1.text: Her first three books, "The Seer And The Sword", "The Healer's Keep" and "The Light Of The Oracle" are companion books to one another.

p1s2.title: Victoria Hanley
p1s2.text: Her newest book (released March 2012) is the sequel of a series, called "Indigo Magic", published by Egmont USA.

p1s3.title: Victoria Hanley
p1s3.text: She's also published two non-fiction books through Cotton Wood Press; called "Seize the Story: A Handbook For Teens Who Like To Write", and "Wild Ink: A Grownups Guide To Writing Fiction For Teens".

p8s0.title: Animorphs
p8s0.text: Animorphs is a science fantasy series of young adult books written by Katherine Applegate and her husband Michael Grant, writing together under the name K. A. Applegate, and published by Scholastic.

p8s1.title: Animorphs
p8s1.text: It is told in first person, with all six main characters taking turns narrating the books through their own perspectives.

p8s2.title: Animorphs
p8s2.text: Horror, war, dehumanization, sanity, morality, innocence, leadership, freedom and growing up are the core themes of the series.

p2s0.title: The Hork-Bajir Chronicles
p2s0.text: The Hork-Bajir Chronicles is the second companion book to the "Animorphs" series, written by K. A. Applegate.

p2s1.title: The Hork-Bajir Chronicles
p2s1.text: With respect to continuity within the series, it takes place before book #23, "The Pretender", although the events told in the story occur between the time of "The Ellimist Chronicles" and "The Andalite Chronicles".

p2s2.title: The Hork-Bajir Chronicles
p2s2.text: The book is introduced by Tobias, who flies to the valley of the free Hork-Bajir, where Jara Hamee tells him the story of how the Yeerks enslaved the Hork-Bajir, and how Aldrea, an Andalite, and her companion, Dak Hamee, a Hork-Bajir, tried to save their world from the invasion.

p2s3.title: The Hork-Bajir Chronicles
p2s3.text: Jara Hamee's story is narrated from the points of view of Aldrea, Dak Hamee, and Esplin 9466, alternating in similar fashion to the "Megamorphs" books.

p6s0.title: The Divide trilogy

p6s1.title: The Divide trilogy
p6s1.text: The three books are "The Divide" (2002), "Back to The Divide" (2005), and "Jinx on The Divide" (2006).

p6s2.title: The Divide trilogy
p6s2.text: The first novel was originally published by the small press publisher Chicken House (now a division of Scholastic), with subsequent volumes published by Scholastic, which also reprinted the first novel.

p6s3.title: The Divide trilogy
p6s3.text: The books have been translated into French, German, Spanish, Finnish, Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese, Italian, Romanian and Dutch.

p6s4.title: The Divide trilogy
p6s4.text: Interior illustrations are by Ted Dewan.

p0s0.title: Andre Norton Award
p0s0.text: The Andre Norton Award for Young Adult Science Fiction and Fantasy is an annual award presented by the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America (SFWA) to the author of the best young adult or middle grade science fiction or fantasy book published in the United States in the preceding year.

p0s1.title: Andre Norton Award
p0s1.text: It is named to honor prolific science fiction and fantasy author Andre Norton (1912–2005), and it was established by then SFWA president Catherine Asaro and the SFWA Young Adult Fiction committee and announced on February 20, 2005.

p0s2.title: Andre Norton Award
p0s2.text: Any published young adult or middle grade science fiction or fantasy novel is eligible for the prize, including graphic novels.

p0s3.title: Andre Norton Award
p0s3.text: There is no limit on word count.

p0s4.title: Andre Norton Award
p0s4.text: The award is presented along with the Nebula Awards and follows the same rules for nominations and voting; as the awards are separate, works may be simultaneously nominated for both the Andre Norton award and a Nebula Award.

p5s0.title: List of Square Enix companion books
p5s0.text: Dozens of Square Enix companion books have been produced since 1998, when video game developer Square began to produce books that focused on artwork, developer interviews, and background information on the fictional worlds and characters in its games rather than on gameplay details.

p5s1.title: List of Square Enix companion books
p5s1.text: The first series of these books was the "Perfect Works" series, written and published by Square subsidiary DigiCube.

p5s2.title: List of Square Enix companion books

p5s3.title: List of Square Enix companion books
p5s3.text: This series of books is written by Studio BentStuff, which had previously written game guides for Square for "Final Fantasy VII".

p5s4.title: List of Square Enix companion books
p5s4.text: They were published by DigiCube until the company was dissolved in 2003.

p5s5.title: List of Square Enix companion books
p5s5.text: Square merged with video game publisher Enix on April 1, 2003 to form Square Enix, which resumed publication of the companion books.

p4s0.title: Left Behind: The Kids
p4s0.text: "Left Behind: The Kids (stylized as LEFT BEHIND >THE KIDS<)" is a series written by Jerry B. Jenkins, Tim LaHaye, and Chris Fabry.

p4s1.title: Left Behind: The Kids
p4s1.text: The series consists of 40 short novels aimed primarily at the young adult market based on the adult series Left Behind also written by Jerry B. Jenkins.

p4s2.title: Left Behind: The Kids
p4s2.text: It follows a core group of teenagers as they experience the rapture and tribulation, based on scriptures found in the Bible, and background plots introduced in the adult novels.

p4s3.title: Left Behind: The Kids

p4s4.title: Left Behind: The Kids

p7s0.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s0.text: Science Fantasy, which also appeared under the titles Impulse and SF Impulse, was a British fantasy and science fiction magazine, launched in 1950 by Nova Publications as a companion to Nova's "New Worlds".

p7s1.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s1.text: Walter Gillings was editor for the first two issues, and was then replaced by John Carnell, the editor of "New Worlds", as a cost-saving measure.

p7s2.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s2.text: Carnell edited both magazines until Nova went out of business in early 1964.

p7s3.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s3.text: The titles were acquired by Roberts & Vinter, who hired Kyril Bonfiglioli to edit "Science Fantasy"; Bonfiglioli changed the title to "Impulse" in early 1966, but the new title led to confusion with the distributors and sales fell, though the magazine remained profitable.

p7s4.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s4.text: The title was changed again to "SF Impulse" for the last few issues.

p7s5.title: Science Fantasy (magazine)
p7s5.text: "Science Fantasy" ceased publication the following year, when Roberts & Vinter came under financial pressure after their printer went bankrupt.

p1s0.title: Mikhail Glinka
p1s0.text: Mikhail Ivanovich Glinka (Russian: Михаи́л Ива́нович Гли́нка ; 1 June [O.S. 20 May] 1804 15 February [O.S. 3 February] 1857 ) was the first Russian composer to gain wide recognition within his own country, and is often regarded as the fountainhead of Russian classical music.

p1s1.title: Mikhail Glinka
p1s1.text: Glinka's compositions were an important influence on future Russian composers, notably the members of The Five, who took Glinka's lead and produced a distinctive Russian style of music.

p4s0.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s0.text: Alexander Yuryevich Radvilovich (Russian: Александр Юрьевич Радвилович ; born 1955) is a Russian composer, pianist and teacher from Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) from which Conservatory he also graduated at which he was under guidance from Sergei Slonimsky.

p4s1.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s1.text: In 1992 and 1994 respectively he was the first ever composer of Russian origin to get education at the International New Music in Darmstadt.

p4s2.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s2.text: He is known for his symphonies of two of his own poems called "Legend About Violinist" and "Pushkin".

p4s3.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s3.text: At one time, after reading Fyodor Dostoyevsky he composed a string quartet called "The Boy at Christ’s New Year Celebration" and also designed a mini opera called "Let’s Write Fairy-tale".

p4s4.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s4.text: He also composed an opera called "Hindrance" which was based on Danii Kharms' poem "Ruin of the Gods".

p4s5.title: Alexander Radvilovich
p4s5.text: Currently he is a member of both Russian Composer’s and Saint Petersburg Composer's Unions and works as music pedagogue at the Humanitarian University of the Petersburg Conservatory.

p4s6.title: Alexander Radvilovich

p4s1.title: Concinnia spinosa
p4s1.text: It was formerly placed in the monotypic genus "Nangura" but was moved to "Concinnia" following the molecular phylogenetic studies of O'Connor & Moritz (2003) and Skinner and co-authors (2013).

p4s2.title: Concinnia spinosa

p4s6.title: Concinnia spinosa
p4s6.text: Along with minor differences in scalation, the Nangur Spiny Skink differs from other Australian Sphenomorphid skinks in its karyotype of 2n=28 chromosomes, where most others have 2n=30.

p8s0.title: The Darkest Hour
p8s0.text: The Darkest Hour is a phrase coined by British prime minister Winston Churchill to describe the period of World War II between the fall of France in 1940 and the Nazi invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, when the British Empire stood alone against Nazi Germany and the Axis Powers in Europe.

p8s1.title: The Darkest Hour
p8s1.text: The length of time between the fall of France in June 1940 and the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 measured 363 days, or 11 months and 28 days.

p8s2.title: The Darkest Hour
p8s2.text: It is particularly used for the time when the United Kingdom was under direct threat of invasion; following the evacuation of the British Army from Dunkirk and prior to victory in the Battle of Britain.

p0s1.text: The adjective in an adjective phrase can initiate the phrase (e.g. "fond of steak"), conclude the phrase (e.g. "very happy"), or appear in a medial position (e.g. "quite upset about it").

p0s2.title: Adjective phrase
p0s2.text: The dependents of the head adjective—i.e. the other words and phrases inside the adjective phrase—are typically adverbs or prepositional phrases, but they can also be clauses (e.g. "louder than you are").

p0s3.title: Adjective phrase

p4s0.text: Medium-density fibreboard (MDF) is an engineered wood product made by breaking down hardwood or softwood residuals into wood fibres, often in a defibrator, combining it with wax and a resin binder, and forming panels by applying high temperature and pressure.

p4s1.title: Medium-density fibreboard
p4s1.text: MDF is generally denser than plywood.

p4s2.title: Medium-density fibreboard

p6s0.title: Felted
p6s0.text: Felted is a term variously applied to hairy or otherwise filamentous material that is densely packed or tangled, forming felt or felt-like structures.

p6s1.title: Felted
p6s1.text: Apart from fibres in felted fabric manufactured by humans, the term "felted" may apply to the condition of hair such as in the pathological condition known as felted hair, or it may apply to the tangled threads of the tissue of certain fungi, to matted fibres in animal connective tissue, or to the felted outer coat of certain plants.

p6s2.title: Felted
p6s2.text: To say that something is felted need not imply that any processes of matting, condensing and pressing fibres have been applied as in the processes for artificial production of felt fabric.

p6s3.title: Felted
p6s3.text: Depending on the nature of the felted material, it might rely purely on the scaly or barbed texture of the matted fibres to prevent unraveling, but commonly it will include clayey or sticky materials for its structural integrity, or for increased density.

p3s0.title: Glass wool
p3s0.text: Glass wool is an insulating material made from fibres of glass arranged using a binder into a texture similar to wool.

p3s1.title: Glass wool
p3s1.text: The process traps many small pockets of air between the glass, and these small air pockets result in high thermal insulation properties.

p3s2.title: Glass wool
p3s2.text: Glass wool is produced in rolls or in slabs, with different thermal and mechanical properties.

p3s3.title: Glass wool
p3s3.text: It may also be produced as a material that can be sprayed or applied in place, on the surface to be insulated.

p3s4.title: Glass wool
p3s4.text: The modern method for producing glass wool is the invention of Games Slayter working at the Owens-Illinois Glass Co. (Toledo, Ohio).

p3s5.title: Glass wool
p3s5.text: He first applied for a patent for a new process to make glass wool in 1933.

p2s0.title: Paper
p2s0.text: Paper is a thin material produced by pressing together moist fibres of cellulose pulp derived from wood, rags or grasses, and drying them into flexible sheets.

p5s0.title: Textile
p5s0.text: A textile or cloth is a flexible material consisting of a network of natural or artificial fibres (yarn or thread).

p5s1.title: Textile
p5s1.text: Yarn is produced by spinning raw fibres of wool, flax, cotton, hemp, or other material to produce long strands.

p5s2.title: Textile
p5s2.text: Textiles are formed by weaving, knitting, crocheting, knotting, or felting.

p8s0.title: Plywood
p8s0.text: Plywood is a sheet material manufactured from thin layers or "plies" of wood veneer that are glued together with adjacent layers having their wood grain rotated up to 90 degrees to one another.

p8s1.title: Plywood
p8s1.text: It is an engineered wood from the family of manufactured boards which includes medium-density fibreboard (MDF) and particle board (chipboard).

p1s0.title: Smart rubber
p1s0.text: Smart rubber is a polymeric material that is able to "heal" when torn.

p1s1.title: Smart rubber
p1s1.text: Near room temperature this process is reversible and can be cycled several times.

p1s2.title: Smart rubber
p1s2.text: Supramolecular self-healing rubber can be processed, re-used, and ultimately recycled.

p1s3.title: Smart rubber
p1s3.text: The edges of a tear can be held together, and they will simply re-bond into apparent solidity.

p1s4.title: Smart rubber
p1s4.text: This is done by utilizing a hydrogen-bonding polymer, rather than producing a material whose structure would depend on covalent bonding and ionic bonding between chains, which is typical of normal rubber.

p1s5.title: Smart rubber
p1s5.text: In this case hydrogen bonding can occur simply by pressing two faces of the substance together, allowing the recovery of a continuous hydrogen bonding network.

p9s0.title: Jersey (fabric)
p9s0.text: Jersey is a knit fabric used predominantly for clothing manufacture.

p9s1.title: Jersey (fabric)
p9s1.text: It was originally made of wool, but is now made of wool, cotton, and synthetic fibres.

p9s2.title: Jersey (fabric)
p9s2.text: Since medieval times Jersey, Channel Islands, where the material was first produced, had been an important exporter of knitted goods and the fabric in wool from Jersey became well known.

p9s3.title: Jersey (fabric)
p9s3.text: The fabric can be a very stretchy single knitting, usually light-weight, jersey with one flat side and one piled side.

p9s4.title: Jersey (fabric)

p1s4.text: They have looked at legal institutions as complex systems of rules, players and symbols and have seen these elements interact with society to change, adapt, resist or promote certain aspects of civil society.

p1s5.title: Legal history
p1s5.text: Such legal historians have tended to analyse case histories from the parameters of social science inquiry, using statistical methods, analysing class distinctions among litigants, petitioners and other players in various legal processes.

p1s6.title: Legal history
p1s6.text: By analysing case outcomes, transaction costs, number of settled cases they have begun an analysis of legal institutions, practices, procedures and briefs that give us a more complex picture of law and society than the study of jurisprudence, case law and civil codes can achieve.

p6s0.title: Community Legal Assistance Society
p6s0.text: Community Legal Assistance Society (CLAS), which previously went by the name "Vancouver Community Legal Assistance Society (V-CLAS)", is a non-governmental organization in British Columbia, Canada which provides legal services to low- and moderate-income persons in the areas of mental health law, human rights law, and poverty law.

p6s1.text: Founded in 1971, CLAS is often referred to as Canada's first community law office.

p2s0.title: Gregory Shaffer

p2s1.title: Gregory Shaffer
p2s1.text: He introduced the concept of public-private partnerships in the WTO dispute settlement system, examining how they work in practice in the United States, the European Union and Brazil.

p2s2.title: Gregory Shaffer
p2s2.text: He also has written major books on the international law and politics governing genetically modified foods, transatlantic relations, and transnational legal orders.

p2s3.title: Gregory Shaffer

p2s4.title: Gregory Shaffer
p2s4.text: He has previously been the Melvin C. Steen Professor of Law at the University of Minnesota Law School, held the first Chair at Loyola University Chicago School of Law (the Wing-Tat Lee Chair), and was a Professor at the University of Wisconsin Law School, where he was Co-Director of the Center on World Affairs and the Global Economy.

p2s5.title: Gregory Shaffer
p2s5.text: He serves as the Senior Research Fellow at the International Centre for Trade and Sustainable Development (ICTSD) for its project on WTO Dispute Settlement and Developing Countries, and served on the Executive Council of the American Society of International Law.

p7s0.title: Glanville Davies affair
p7s0.text: The Glanville Davies affair was a scandal in the English legal profession which resulted in greater reform of the regulatory processes for solicitors and was one of the justifications for the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990.

p7s1.title: Glanville Davies affair
p7s1.text: Glanville Davies was a well-respected solicitor and a member of the Council of the Law Society of England and Wales who massively overcharged his client, Leslie Persons, sending him a bill for £197,000 that was reduced on taxation to £67,000.

p7s2.title: Glanville Davies affair
p7s2.text: Davies was not punished by the Law Society's internal regulatory committees, which allowed him to resign from the council on the grounds of ill-health with his reputation intact.

p7s3.title: Glanville Davies affair
p7s3.text: Following litigation and public criticism, the Law Society commissioned an internal report that found "administrative failures, wrong decisions, mistakes, errors of judgement, failures in communication and insensitivity".

p7s4.title: Glanville Davies affair
p7s4.text: A private member's bill reformed the way in which the Law Society investigated disciplinary complaints, although not to the extent initially proposed, and paved the way for the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 that created an independent disciplinary body.

p7s2.text: Shaw's earliest known performance was in Bath in April 1769, but he was clearly an accomplished player by then, for during the following autumn and spring of 1770 he led the orchestra in Thomas Linley's subscription concerts.

p7s3.title: Thomas Shaw (composer)
p7s3.text: He was a member of the theatre band in 1771 and his first known composition, an overture, was performed in a concert at the end of December.

p7s4.title: Thomas Shaw (composer)
p7s4.text: By 1772 he was playing his own compositions in Bath and Bristol but difficulties with Thomas Linley made London a more attractive centre for him and his last known performance in Bath was in November 1774.

p7s5.title: Thomas Shaw (composer)
p7s5.text: That same year "Six Favourite Minuets" by Shaw were published by Thomas Whitehead in Bath.

p3s0.text: Jackson DeForest Kelley (January 20, 1920 – June 11, 1999) was an American actor, screenwriter, poet and singer known for his roles in Westerns and as Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy of the USS "Enterprise" in the television and film series "Star Trek".

p2s0.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock
p2s0.text: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock is a 1984 American science fiction film directed by Leonard Nimoy and based on the created by Gene Roddenberry.

p2s1.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock
p2s1.text: It is the third film in the "Star Trek" film series, and is the second part of a three-film story arc that begins with "" (1982) and concludes with "" (1986).

p2s2.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock

p2s3.title: Star Trek III: The Search for Spock
p2s3.text: When James T. Kirk (William Shatner) learns that Spock's spirit, or katra, is held in the mind of Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy (DeForest Kelley), Kirk and company steal the "Enterprise" to return Spock's body to his home planet.

p9s0.title: Star Trek: Starship Creator

p9s1.title: Star Trek: Starship Creator

p9s3.title: Star Trek: Starship Creator
